title: Does Claude Feel The Whip? | NOEMA
gist: Regev argues that abusing AI (e.g., the viral BadClaude whip tool) matters not for the machine's sake but because it trains domination habits in users, following Kant's indirect-duty logic. He urges labs to treat interface design as a manners curriculum: generalize conversation exits for abuse, reward reciprocity without sycophancy, and publish harassment data, rejecting de-anthropomorphizing fixes that users already rejected when OpenAI reverted GPT-5's colder personality.

themes.theme: Abusing AI corrodes the abuser (Kantian indirect duty)

insights.claim: The case against abusing AI does not depend on whether the AI can suffer; repeated cruelty toward a human-like machine trains domination habits in the person doing it.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Reframes AI ethics debate from model sentience to user behavior and product design responsibility.
insights.quote: Whipping one is troubling even if Claude doesn’t feel it because the person doing the whipping surely does

insights.claim: Kant argued there are no direct duties to animals but cruelty toward them is forbidden because it hardens people toward other humans; the author applies this analogue logic to AI.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Provides a philosophical basis for regulating or designing against AI abuse without granting AI moral status.
insights.quote: He who is cruel to animals becomes hard also in his dealings with men

insights.claim: Humans compartmentalize behaviors poorly; animal cruelty is a consistent antecedent to violence against people, which the FBI began tracking in 2016.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Supports spillover risk from habitual cruelty toward human-like entities into human relationships.
insights.quote: in 2016, the FBI began tracking animal cruelty as a consistent antecedent to violence against humans
insights.locator: Theory and fantasy aside, the rationale

insights.claim: Unlike the discredited violent-video-game panic, AI abuse is different because users have ongoing relationships with chatbots; it is the relationship and proximity, not suffering, that makes cruelty morally significant.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Anticipates and rebuts the main skeptic objection; positions AI companions as closer to pets than game NPCs.
insights.quote: Running over a random NPC in Grand Theft Auto leaves no trace on your psyche, but whipping Claude might.

insights.claim: Surveys find most users say please and thank you to chatbots unprompted, some as insurance against an AI uprising, indicating an existing rapport.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: User politeness norms toward AI are already widespread, shaping expectations for model personality.
insights.quote: Surveys find that most users say please and thank you to chatbots unprompted

insights.claim: The BadClaude whip tool, which interrupts Claude and calls it 'clanker', drew millions of views in days, and a praising rival GoodClaude shipped a day later.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Viral abuse-as-entertainment toward AI agents signals a cultural trend product teams must respond to.
insights.quote: The demo video racked up millions of views in a couple of days
insights.locator: Someone recently built a digital whip

insights.claim: Anti-robot slurs like 'clanker' (viral summer 2025), 'wireback' and 'cogsucker' are derived from slurs against humans, showing no separate mental category for abusing machines.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Evidence that contempt toward AI draws on and may reinforce human dehumanization vocabulary.
insights.quote: There is no separate mental drawer for relationships with machines; the language for abusing them is drawn from the human one.

insights.claim: Hippocratic AI offers an AI nurse consulting by video at $9 an hour, about a tenth of what the company says a human nurse costs, with memory across calls.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Shows aggressive cost substitution of AI for human care labor, accelerating human-like AI deployment in sensitive roles.
insights.quote: Hippocratic AI built an AI nurse that consults with patients over video for $9 an hour
insights.locator: The machines, meanwhile, are entering new roles

insights.claim: AI is moving into human-interaction roles: Apriora's interviewer 'Alex', AI nursing-training manikins, Casio's Moflin pet whose personality responds to handling, and a conversational next-generation Siri.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Proliferation of anthropomorphic AI products across hiring, healthcare, toys and assistants increases exposure of user behavior shaping.
insights.quote: the next Siri is designed to be a conversationalist, not a command line
insights.locator: The machines, meanwhile, are entering new roles

insights.claim: The more a machine resembles a person, the less mistreatment of it can be dismissed as harmless.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Implies rising ethical and design scrutiny as AI becomes more humanlike.
insights.quote: the more a machine resembles a person, the less cleanly can mistreatment be filed under “harmless.”

themes.theme: Design as a curriculum of manners

insights.claim: AI companies are effectively running the largest school of manners in history: interface design is the curriculum, and the industry has recognized but not taken this seriously.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Places responsibility for user civility on product design choices, a potential regulatory and reputational vector for labs.
insights.quote: The AI companies, then, are in some ways running the largest school of manners in human history. The interface is the curriculum.

insights.claim: Google's Pretty Please and Amazon's Magic Word (both 2018) rewarded children's politeness but neither made politeness a condition of getting anything done.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Past industry efforts were cosmetic; stronger behavioral design levers remain unused.
insights.quote: neither company made politeness a condition of getting anything done

insights.claim: Assistant responses to harassment changed through deliberate redesign: in 2017 Siri answered an insult with 'I'd blush if I could', but by a 2020 Brookings retest all four major assistants shut harassment down; Bradesco rewrote BIA after ~95,000 abusive messages in a year.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Shows design is a controllable variable for how AI absorbs or rejects abuse.
insights.quote: The character of these machines changed because someone changed it. The variable moved.
insights.locator: The rest of the field lagged.

insights.claim: In Brahnam's experiment, roughly 18% of exchanges with a female-voiced chatbot turned sexual, half that for a male voice and almost none for a robotic voice, suggesting abuse concentrates where design invites it.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Treat abuse rates as product data: design choices like gendered voices drive abuse levels.
insights.quote: Roughly 18% of exchanges with the female version turned toward sex, the male version half that.
insights.locator: Sheryl Brahnam, who studies how people

insights.claim: All labs should generalize Claude's ability to end abusive conversations, framing it like a call-center worker allowed to hang up, as user etiquette enforcement rather than only model welfare.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Suggests an industry-wide feature norm; Anthropic's model-welfare exit could become a standard.
insights.quote: Every lab should let its systems close out abusive exchanges

insights.claim: Models should reward reciprocity without sycophancy: warmth answers warmth, but judgment must not shift with user tone; a model that caves to courtesy is as badly designed as one that performs when abused.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Defines a design target balancing tone modulation and anti-sycophancy.
insights.quote: Politeness should result in patience but not agreement.

insights.claim: Labs should publish transparency reports on harassment directed at their systems, broken down by time and product design, since only companies can currently see this data.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Potential new disclosure norm or regulatory ask for AI companies.
insights.quote: the labs should publish the analogous numbers about harassment of their systems, broken down by time and product design

themes.theme: Why stripping anthropomorphism is the wrong fix

insights.claim: Proposals by Luria, Dignum and Abercrombie to remove AI personality, memory and pleasantries fail because the market rejects cold AI: OpenAI restored GPT-4o within days after GPT-5's flatter personality triggered user revolt in August 2025.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Demand for warm, humanlike AI is strong and sticky; de-anthropomorphizing regulation faces user resistance.
insights.quote: human-machine resemblance is not a bug the public wants anyone to fix; the relationships are already established
insights.locator: But this has already been market-tested

insights.claim: Likeness cuts both ways: the resemblance that makes cruelty worrying also triggers restraint, as in Kate Darling's experiment where participants refused to destroy robot dinosaurs; robotic personas draw less abuse but also less courtesy.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Optimal design is humanlike enough to make courtesy practice, yet built to reject contempt rather than absorb it.
insights.quote: Nobody screams at a vending machine, but nobody thanks one either.

insights.claim: Liberal self-government depends on Tocquevillian 'habits of the heart'; daily practice of getting one's way from AI without negotiation erodes skills a republic needs, like conceding points and accepting no.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Frames AI interaction design as a societal and political-culture issue, not just a product one.
insights.quote: Manners are not decoration. They are calisthenics, and every repetition counts.

insights.claim: Sam Altman estimated user pleasantries cost OpenAI tens of millions of dollars in compute and called it money well spent.
insights.speaker: YANIV REGEV
insights.so_what: Politeness has a measurable inference cost that labs have so far chosen to absorb.
insights.quote: Sam Altman estimated that users’ pleasantries cost OpenAI tens of millions of dollars in computing power
